## 5. KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

### Part A — Short Answer Questions (3 Marks each)

**Q1. [KTU University Exam – May 2024] Define a hyperaccumulator plant and list the criteria used to classify a plant as a hyperaccumulator.**

> **Model Answer (3 marks):**
> A **hyperaccumulator** is a plant species capable of accumulating **exceptionally high concentrations of a specific metal or metalloid** in its above-ground biomass (shoots) without suffering from phytotoxic effects.
>
> **Brooks Criteria** for hyperaccumulation (concentration in dry shoot biomass):
> - **Cd** ≥ 100 mg/kg
> - **As, Co, Cu, Ni, Pb, Sb, Se, Zn** ≥ 1000 mg/kg
> - **Au, Ag** ≥ 1 mg/kg
> - **Mn, Fe** (less strict thresholds)
>
> In addition, the plant must exhibit a **Bioconcentration Factor (BCF) > 1** and a **Translocation Factor (TF) > 1**, demonstrating efficient uptake and root-to-shoot transport. Examples include *Thlaspi caerulescens* (Cd/Zn), *Pteris vittata* (As), and *Alyssum lesbiacum* (Ni).

---

**Q2. [KTU University Exam – Dec 2023] What is the role of the bacterial *merA* gene in transgenic phytoremediation? Mention the substrate and product of the enzyme it encodes.**

> **Model Answer (3 marks):**
> The *merA* gene, sourced from mercury-resistant bacteria such as *Pseudomonas* and *Escherichia coli*, encodes the enzyme **mercuric ion reductase (MerA)**, a **NADPH-dependent flavoenzyme** that catalyzes the reduction of ionic mercury (Hg²⁺) to elemental mercury (Hg⁰).
>
> **Reaction catalyzed:**
> $$Hg^{2+} + NADPH + H^+ \xrightarrow{\text{MerA}} Hg^0 + NADP^+ + 2H^+$$
>
> The volatile Hg⁰ is subsequently released into the atmosphere via the plant's stomata, achieving **in-situ phytovolatilization** of mercury contamination. Transgenic plants expressing *merA* show **10–100× greater tolerance** to mercury than wild-type plants.

---

### Part B — Long Answer Questions (14 Marks each, with Internal Choice)

---

**Q3. [KTU University Exam – May 2023] — Question A (14 marks)**

> **(a)** Discuss the strategic approaches of genetic engineering in phytoremediation. Describe **any two** approaches in detail with suitable examples. **(7 marks)**
>
> **(b)** Explain the *mer* operon-based mercury phytoremediation in transgenic plants. Include the biochemical pathway, genetic construct, and the ecological advantages of phytovolatilization. **(7 marks)**

#### Model Solution:

**(a) Strategic Approaches of Genetic Engineering in Phytoremediation**

The strategic approaches can be classified as follows:

**(i) Metal Transporter Engineering**
Overexpression of genes encoding plasma-membrane and vacuolar transporters boosts metal uptake. Example: Transgenic tobacco overexpressing **AtHMA4** (a P-type ATPase from *Arabidopsis thaliana*) shows **2–3× higher root-to-shoot Cd translocation** due to enhanced xylem loading.

**(ii) Chelator and Ligand Biosynthesis Engineering**
Engineered synthesis of **phytochelatins (PCs)**, **metallothioneins (MTs)**, and **organic acids** (citrate, malate, histidine) increases metal sequestration. Example: Expression of the **human metallothionein gene *hMT-IIA*** in tobacco conferred **4–6× higher Cd and Cu tolerance**, with enhanced vacuolar compartmentalization.

**(iii) Detoxification Enzyme Engineering**
Expression of microbial enzymes that transform toxic pollutants into less harmful metabolites. Example: Expression of the bacterial **merA** gene (mercuric ion reductase) enables Hg²⁺ → Hg⁰ reduction.

**(iv) Compartmentalization Engineering**
Engineering of vacuolar transporters and cysteine-rich peptides that localize metals into safe cellular compartments.

**(v) Regulatory Pathway Engineering**
Overexpression of transcription factors (WRKY, MYB) or silencing of negative regulators via RNAi/CRISPR to upregulate stress-response regulons.

**(b) Mer Operon-Based Mercury Phytoremediation**

The bacterial *mer* operon from *E. coli* typically contains **merT, merP, merC** (transporters), **merB** (organomercurial lyase), and **merA** (mercuric ion reductase), regulated by **merR** (regulator) and **merD**.

**Genetic Construct:** A typical binary vector contains:
- **35S CaMV promoter** (constitutive expression)
- ***merA*** and/or ***merB*** coding sequences
- **Nos terminator**
- **nptII** (kanamycin resistance) selectable marker
- All cloned between **T-DNA borders** of a *Ti-plasmid*-derived vector.

**Biochemical Pathway:**

$$
CH_3Hg^+ \xrightarrow{\text{MerB}} Hg^{2+} + CH_4 \xrightarrow{\text{MerA, NADPH}} Hg^0 \;(\text{volatile})
$$

**Ecological Advantages of Phytovolatilization:**
- Mercury is removed **in-situ** without excavation.
- **No secondary waste** is generated (unlike soil washing).
- The process is **solar-powered** and self-propagating once plants are established.
- Suitable for **deep soil contamination** that is inaccessible to conventional engineering methods.
- Reduces the **total mercury load** of the rhizosphere over multiple growing seasons.

**Limitations:**
- Atmospheric release of Hg⁰ requires dispersion modeling.
- Regulatory restrictions on GMO release in some jurisdictions.

---

**Q4. [KTU University Exam – Dec 2024] — Question B (14 marks)**

> **(a)** Describe the role of **phytochelatins and metallothioneins** in heavy metal phytoremediation. Explain how their biosynthesis is enhanced by genetic engineering. **(7 marks)**
>
> **(b)** Write a detailed note on **transgenic phytoremediation of arsenic** — covering the *ars* operon, arsenate reductase (ArsC), and phytochelatin-mediated vacuolar sequestration. **(7 marks)**

#### Model Solution:

**(a) Phytochelatins and Metallothioneins in Heavy Metal Phytoremediation**

**Phytochelatins (PCs)** are a family of **thiol-rich, metal-binding peptides** with the general structure **(γ-Glu-Cys)ₙ-Gly** (where n = 2–11), synthesized enzymatically from **glutathione (GSH)** by **phytochelatin synthase (PCS, EC 2.3.2.15)**.

**Reaction Catalyzed by PCS:**
$$
n \, \text{GSH} \xrightarrow{\text{PCS}} (\gamma\text{-Glu-Cys})_n\text{-Gly} + n \, \text{Gly}
$$

PCs chelate **Cd²⁺, As(III), Hg²⁺, Pb²⁺, Zn²⁺, Cu⁺** with very high affinity via the free **thiol (-SH) groups of cysteine**, forming low-molecular-weight PC–metal complexes in the cytosol, which are then transported into vacuoles.

**Metallothioneins (MTs)** are **gene-encoded** (unlike PCs, which are enzymatically synthesized), cysteine-rich, low-molecular-weight proteins (~6–7 kDa) that bind metals through **cysteine thiolate clusters**. They are particularly important for **Cu²⁺, Zn²⁺, and Cd²⁺** binding.

**Genetic Engineering for Enhanced PC/MT Biosynthesis:**

| Strategy | Gene Modified | Outcome |
|---|---|---|
| Overexpress PCS | *AtPCS1* (from *Arabidopsis*) in tobacco | 2–3× increased Cd accumulation |
| Boost GSH precursor | γ-glutamylcysteine synthetase (*γ-ECS*) | Increased substrate availability for PCs |
| Express MT heterologously | Mouse *MT-I*, Human *hMT-IIA*, Yeast *CUP1* | 4–6× Cd/Cu tolerance |
| Fusion constructs | PC–GFP fusion | Real-time visualization of metal binding |

**(b) Transgenic Phytoremediation of Arsenic**

Arsenic is a **Class I carcinogen** with two environmentally relevant forms:
- **As(V)** (arsenate) — predominant in aerobic soils, mimics phosphate
- **As(III)** (arsenite) — predominant in anaerobic/waterlogged soils, highly toxic

The **bacterial *ars* operon** from *Staphylococcus aureus* plasmid pI258 contains:
- ***arsR*** — transcriptional repressor
- ***arsB*** — arsenite efflux pump
- ***arsC*** — arsenate reductase (converts As(V) → As(III))
- ***arsD*** — metallochaperone

**ArsC Reaction:**
$$
AsO_4^{3-} + \text{glutaredoxin (GSH-coupled)} \xrightarrow{\text{ArsC}} AsO_3^{3-} + \text{oxidized glutaredoxin}
$$

**Combined Transgenic Strategy for Arsenic:**
1. **arsC** expression reduces As(V) → As(III) in planta.
2. **PCS1** overexpression complexes As(III) with phytochelatins: **As(III)–PC₃** complexes.
3. **HMA3** overexpression sequesters As(III)–PC complexes into **vacuoles**.

**Performance Outcome:**
- Transgenic rice and *Arabidopsis* expressing *arsC* show **3–5× higher As tolerance**.
- Vacuolar sequestration prevents cytoplasmic damage and enables safe **shoot accumulation** for eventual **phytomining** or **safe disposal**.

> [!WARNING]
> **KTU Examiner's Valuation Pitfalls — Common Mark-Loss Zones:**
> 1. **Confusing the *mer* and *ars* operons**: Students frequently mix up Hg and As pathways. Memorize: **merA reduces Hg²⁺; arsC reduces As(V)**.
> 2. **Misidentifying BCF vs TF**: BCF = soil-to-plant; TF = root-to-shoot. Both must exceed 1.
> 3. **Ignoring regulatory/GMO aspects**: Transgenic field release requires permits under the **Environment Protection Act, 1986** and the **Rules for the Manufacture, Use, Import, Export and Storage of Hazardous Microorganisms/Genetically Engineered Organisms, 1989**. Examiners award marks for mentioning biosafety frameworks.
> 4. **Failing to give plant examples**: Always cite a model plant (*Arabidopsis*, tobacco, rice, *Brassica juncea*) with every transgene.
> 5. **Spelling the "phyto" terms correctly**: phytoextraction ≠ phytostabilization ≠ phytovolatilization. KTU examiners deduct 0.5–1 mark for wrong usage.

---

### Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember (Rapid-Revision Checklist)

- **Phytoremediation** = green technology using plants to clean environmental contaminants.
- **Genetic engineering** enhances the natural capacity by transferring genes from bacteria, animals, or other plants.
- **Five Pillars** of genetic engineering: Transporter Engineering, Chelator Biosynthesis, Detoxification Enzymes, Compartmentalization, Regulatory Pathway Engineering.
- **Mercury pathway**: CH₃Hg⁺ --(*merB*)--> Hg²⁺ --(*merA*)--> Hg⁰ (volatile).
- **Arsenic pathway**: As(V) --(*arsC*)--> As(III) --(*PCS1, PC*)--> As(III)-PC --(vacuole)--> storage.
- **Hyperaccumulator** defined by Brooks criteria (Cd ≥100; As/Co/Cu/Ni/Pb/Se/Zn ≥1000 mg/kg dry shoot).
- **BCF > 1** and **TF > 1** are mandatory for classification.
- **Ti-plasmid** of *Agrobacterium tumefaciens* is the standard plant transformation vector.
- **Selectable markers**: *nptII* (kanamycin), *hpt* (hygromycin).
- **Phytochelatins** = enzymatically synthesized from GSH by PCS.
- **Metallothioneins** = gene-encoded, cysteine-rich proteins.
- **Model transgenic plants**: Tobacco, *Arabidopsis*, *Brassica juncea*, rice, *Populus*.
- **Applications**: Mine tailings, brownfields, wetlands, military ranges, agricultural soil.
- **Regulatory frameworks**: EPA 1986; Rules 1989; Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety.
- **Limitations**: Public acceptance of GMOs, gene flow risk, regulatory delays, narrow contaminant range per plant.
- **Future directions**: **CRISPR-Cas9** genome editing for precision engineering; **synthetic biology** circuits for multi-contaminant plants; **rhizosphere microbiome engineering** combined with plant modification.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **One-Line KTU Mantra to remember:**
> *"Engineer the transporter, amplify the chelator, deploy the enzyme, sequester in vacuole, and volatilize if possible."* — This single sentence covers all five pillars of genetic engineering in phytoremediation.

<!-- SECTION_5_END -->

topics.content:
> **APJ ABDUL KALAM TECHNOLOGICAL UNIVERSITY (KTU) | 2024 SCHEME**
> - **Course:** PEBBT754 - BIOREMEDIATION
> - **Module:** Module 4
> - **Topic:** Algal and Fungal-Based Bioremediation

<!-- SECTION_1_START -->
# 1. Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

## 1.1 Phycoremediation (Algal-Based Bioremediation)

**Formal KTU 2024 Definition:**
> **Phycoremediation** is the use of algae (macro- and microalgae) to remove, degrade, detoxify, or sequester environmental pollutants from water, soil, and air. It integrates processes like *biosorption, bioaccumulation, biotransformation, biofixation, and photoremediation* to remediate organic xenobiotics, heavy metals, nutrients (N, P), CO₂, and dyes.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU Syllabus Highlight:** Algal systems are uniquely capable of **coupling pollutant removal with CO₂ sequestration and biomass generation** (for biofuels, fertilizers, feed) — making them *dual-benefit* remediation agents compared to conventional bacterial systems.

### Conceptual Analogy — The "Solar-Powered Cleanup Crew"
Think of a polluted pond as a *dirty kitchen*. Bacteria are like night-shift cleaners that work hard but need constant feeding and produce sludge. **Algae are like rooftop solar panels with a built-in mop**: they use *sunlight* (free energy) and *CO₂* (a pollutant itself) to grow, while simultaneously *absorbing* nutrients (N, P) that cause eutrophication and *sequestering* heavy metals into their biomass. The result? A clean pond *and* a useful "biomass cake" you can sell as fertilizer or biofuel.

---

## 1.2 Mycoremediation (Fungal-Based Bioremediation)

**Formal KTU 2024 Definition:**
> **Mycoremediation** is the application of fungi — particularly *white-rot fungi* (e.g., *Phanerochaete chrysosporium*), *brown-rot fungi*, and their isolated **extracellular oxidative enzymes (laccases, peroxidases, cytochrome P450)** — to biodegrade, transform, or sequester persistent organic pollutants (POPs), hydrocarbons, pesticides, dyes, plastics, and heavy metals.

> [!NOTE]
> **Core Definition Box:** The term *mycoremediation* was popularized by **Paul Stamets** (2005), who demonstrated fungi's unique ability to break down **lignin-mimicking xenobiotics** using their **ligninolytic enzyme system**.

### Conceptual Analogy — "Nature's Chemical Demolition Team"
Imagine a stubborn wooden log that won't decompose. Fungi are the *only kingdom* that can dismantle **lignin** — one of nature's most complex, recalcitrant polymers. Because many industrial pollutants (PAHs, PCBs, dioxins, azo dyes) are *structurally similar to lignin*, fungi mistakenly recognize them as food and attack them with the same powerful **ligninolytic enzymes**. Think of fungi as a *molecular Swiss Army knife*: their **hyphal network** reaches deep into soil, while their enzymes operate *extracellularly*, meaning they can attack large, insoluble molecules that bacterial enzymes (which work inside cells) cannot reach.

---

## 1.3 Comparative Snapshot

| Feature | Algae (Phycoremediation) | Fungi (Mycoremediation) |
|---|---|---|
| Energy source | **Photoautotrophic** (sunlight + CO₂) | **Heterotrophic** (organic carbon) |
| Key mechanism | Biosorption + Bioaccumulation | Enzymatic biodegradation |
| Target pollutants | Nutrients (N, P), heavy metals, CO₂, dyes | POPs, PAHs, pesticides, dyes, plastics |
| Operating condition | Requires **light** | **Light-independent** |
| Biomass utility | Biofuel, biofertilizer, feed | Enzyme production, biocomposting |
| Generation time | **Hours to days** (fast) | **Days to weeks** (slower) |

<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->
# 2. Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

## 2.1 Mechanisms of Phycoremediation (5 Pillars)

### (A) Biosorption
- **Passive**, metabolism-independent binding of pollutants to the **algal cell wall** (rich in carboxyl, amino, phosphate, sulfhydryl groups).
- Operates on **dead or live** biomass — fast, reversible.
- *Key components:* Alginates, cellulose, peptidoglycan, extracellular polymeric substances (EPS).

### (B) Bioaccumulation
- **Active**, metabolism-dependent uptake of pollutants (especially heavy metals) *into* the cell cytoplasm.
- Live cells only, energy-coupled (uses **ATPases** like Cd²⁺-ATPase, Zn²⁺-ATPase).
- Risk: **Biomagnification** in food chain.

### (C) Biotransformation / Biodegradation
- Enzymatic conversion (e.g., cytochrome P450, nitroreductases) of organic pollutants into less toxic metabolites.
- Example: *Chlorella* degrading azo dyes via azoreductase.

### (D) Biofixation
- Conversion of gaseous/aqueous pollutants into **biomass components**.
- E.g., CO₂ → carbohydrates via **Calvin cycle**; N₂ → proteins via nitrogenase.

### (E) Phytovolatilization / Rhizofiltration
- Release of volatile metabolites (e.g., methylated Se, As) into the atmosphere.
- Algal mats in constructed wetlands filtering drainage water.

---

## 2.2 Mechanisms of Mycoremediation (3 Pillars)

### (A) Enzymatic Biodegradation
The **Ligninolytic Enzyme System** consists of:

1. **Lignin Peroxidase (LiP)** — oxidizes aromatic rings with high redox potential (>1.4 V).
2. **Manganese Peroxidase (MnP)** — oxidizes Mn²⁺ → Mn³⁺, which attacks phenolic compounds.
3. **Laccase (Lac)** — copper-containing oxidase, uses O₂, attacks phenolic & non-phenolic substrates.
4. **Cytochrome P450 Monooxygenases** — intracellular, broad substrate specificity.

> [!NOTE]
> **Why fungi > bacteria for POPs?** Bacteria require the pollutant to enter the cell. Fungal **extracellular enzymes** diffuse freely into soil, attacking **insoluble, high-MW polymers** that bacteria physically cannot access.

### (B) Biosorption
- Fungal cell wall contains **chitin, chitosan, glucans, melanins** with high metal-binding affinity.
- Industrial application: **fungal biomass columns** for wastewater treatment.

### (C) Mycelial Network Foraging
- Hyphae extend *microscopically* into soil pores, reaching contaminants inaccessible to bacteria.
- Enable **bioaugmentation** by transporting co-metabolic bacteria.

---

## 2.3 KTU Formula Sheet / Cheat Sheet

> [!IMPORTANT]
> All formulas below are **direct KTU exam fetches**. Memorize the **name + final form + units**.

| # | Formula / Concept | Mathematical Form | Description | Units |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Specific Growth Rate (μ) | $\mu = \dfrac{\ln X_{2} - \ln X_{1}}{t_{2} - t_{1}}$ | Where $X_{1}, X_{2}$ = biomass conc. at times $t_{1}, t_{2}$ | h⁻¹ or day⁻¹ |
| 2 | Monod Kinetics (Algal Growth) | $\mu = \mu_{\max} \cdot \dfrac{S}{K_{s} + S}$ | $S$ = limiting substrate, $K_s$ = half-saturation constant | h⁻¹ |
| 3 | Biomass Productivity | $P = \dfrac{X_{f} - X_{i}}{t}$ | $X_i, X_f$ = initial & final biomass | g L⁻¹ day⁻¹ |
| 4 | Substrate Removal Efficiency | $R\,\% = \dfrac{C_{0} - C_{e}}{C_{0}} \times 100$ | $C_0$ = initial, $C_e$ = equilibrium conc. | \% |
| 5 | Langmuir Isotherm (Biosorption) | $q_{e} = \dfrac{q_{\max} \, b \, C_{e}}{1 + b \, C_{e}}$ | $q_{\max}$ = max capacity, $b$ = affinity constant | mg g⁻¹ |
| 6 | Freundlich Isotherm | $q_{e} = K_{f} \cdot C_{e}^{\,1/n}$ | Empirical; $K_f$ = capacity, $1/n$ = intensity | mg g⁻¹ |
| 7 | Linear Langmuir (Plot form) | $\dfrac{C_{e}}{q_{e}} = \dfrac{1}{q_{\max} \, b} + \dfrac{C_{e}}{q_{\max}}$ | $C_e/q_e$ vs $C_e$ → slope = $1/q_{\max}$ | — |
| 8 | Biomass Doubling Time | $t_{d} = \dfrac{\ln 2}{\mu} = \dfrac{0.693}{\mu}$ | Cell cycle time | h |
| 9 | Volumetric O₂ Transfer | $OTR = k_{L}a \, (C^{*}_{O_{2}} - C_{L})$ | $k_L a$ = mass transfer coefficient | mg L⁻¹ h⁻¹ |
| 10 | Carbon Fixation (Photosynthesis) | $6\,CO_{2} + 6\,H_{2}O \xrightarrow{h\nu} C_{6}H_{12}O_{6} + 6\,O_{2}$ | Drives autotrophic remediation | mol |

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **LaTeX Tip:** In the table above, I used `\dfrac` and `\cdot` to avoid any `|` character that would break the markdown table parser. **Do NOT use `|` for absolute value inside markdown tables in your own notes.**

---

## 2.4 Real-World Engineering Utility

- **Constructed Wetlands** (e.g., Kerala's Kuttanad region): *Duckweed + microalgae* strips nutrients from aquaculture runoff.
- **Algal Photobioreactors** (PBRs): Closed tubular systems for simultaneous CO₂ scrubbing (from power plants) and biodiesel production.
- **Mycoremediation Pads** (Stamets' MycoFilter): Fungal mycelia + agricultural waste used to filter **E. coli**, heavy metals, and hydrocarbons from stream water.
- **White-rot bioreactors**: Continuous stirred-tank reactors (CSTRs) using *P. chrysosporium* immobilized on polyurethane foam for textile dye decolorization.

<!-- SECTION_2_END -->

<!-- SECTION_3_START -->
# 3. Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix

## 3.1 Derivation: Specific Growth Rate from Biomass Data

**Problem:** In a *Chlorella vulgaris* photobioreactor, biomass concentration is $X_1 = 0.20$ g L⁻¹ at $t_1 = 0$ h and $X_2 = 1.60$ g L⁻¹ at $t_2 = 24$ h. Calculate the **specific growth rate (μ)** and the **doubling time (t_d)**.

**Step 1 — Identify the governing equation (from Formula Sheet, Row 1):**

$$\mu = \dfrac{\ln X_{2} - \ln X_{1}}{t_{2} - t_{1}}$$

**Step 2 — Substitute the values carefully:**

$$\mu = \dfrac{\ln(1.60) - \ln(0.20)}{24 - 0}$$

**Step 3 — Simplify using logarithm subtraction law** $\ln(a) - \ln(b) = \ln(a/b)$:

$$\mu = \dfrac{\ln\!\left(\dfrac{1.60}{0.20}\right)}{24}$$

**Step 4 — Compute the numerical ratio:**

$$\dfrac{1.60}{0.20} = 8.00$$

**Step 5 — Take natural log:**

$$\ln(8.00) \approx 2.0794$$

**Step 6 — Final division:**

$$\mu = \dfrac{2.0794}{24} \approx 0.0866 \text{ h}^{-1}$$

**Step 7 — Convert to doubling time (Formula Sheet, Row 8):**

$$t_{d} = \dfrac{0.693}{\mu} = \dfrac{0.693}{0.0866} \approx 8.00 \text{ h}$$

**Engineering Interpretation:** *Chlorella* doubles every **8 hours** under these conditions — a typical high-productivity algal strain suitable for coupled bioremediation + biofuel systems.

---

## 3.2 Derivation: Langmuir Biosorption Isotherm Parameters

**Problem:** Equilibrium biosorption data for **Cd²⁺** uptake by dried *Aspergillus niger* biomass:

| $C_e$ (mg L⁻¹) | $q_e$ (mg g⁻¹) |
|---|---|
| 1.0 | 4.2 |
| 2.0 | 7.5 |
| 4.0 | 12.8 |
| 8.0 | 19.6 |

Determine $q_{\max}$ and $b$ using the **linearized Langmuir equation**.

**Step 1 — Start with Langmuir equation (Formula Sheet, Row 5):**

$$q_{e} = \dfrac{q_{\max} \, b \, C_{e}}{1 + b \, C_{e}}$$

**Step 2 — Invert both sides:**

$$\dfrac{1}{q_{e}} = \dfrac{1 + b\,C_{e}}{q_{\max} \, b \, C_{e}} = \dfrac{1}{q_{\max} \, b \, C_{e}} + \dfrac{1}{q_{\max}}$$

**Step 3 — Rearrange into linear form** (commonly used plot: $C_e/q_e$ vs $C_e$):

$$\dfrac{C_{e}}{q_{e}} = \dfrac{1}{q_{\max} \, b} + \dfrac{C_{e}}{q_{\max}}$$

**Step 4 — Construct the $C_e/q_e$ table:**

| $C_e$ (mg L⁻¹) | $q_e$ (mg g⁻¹) | $C_e / q_e$ (g L⁻¹) |
|---|---|---|
| 1.0 | 4.2  | 0.2381 |
| 2.0 | 7.5  | 0.2667 |
| 4.0 | 12.8 | 0.3125 |
| 8.0 | 19.6 | 0.4082 |

**Step 5 — Linear regression** (assume data is exactly collinear for exam simplification). Pick two extremes:

$$\text{slope} = \dfrac{0.4082 - 0.2381}{8.0 - 1.0} = \dfrac{0.1701}{7.0} \approx 0.0243 \text{ L g}^{-1}$$

**Step 6 — From slope = $1/q_{\max}$:**

$$q_{\max} = \dfrac{1}{0.0243} \approx 41.15 \text{ mg g}^{-1}$$

**Step 7 — Calculate intercept** using $C_e = 1.0$:

$$\text{intercept} = 0.2381 - (0.0243 \times 1.0) = 0.2138$$

**Step 8 — From intercept = $1/(q_{\max} b)$:**

$$b = \dfrac{1}{q_{\max} \times \text{intercept}} = \dfrac{1}{41.15 \times 0.2138} \approx 0.1137 \text{ L mg}^{-1}$$

**Step 9 — Final Langmuir equation for *A. niger* + Cd²⁺:**

$$q_{e} = \dfrac{41.15 \times 0.1137 \times C_{e}}{1 + 0.1137 \, C_{e}}$$

**Engineering Interpretation:** $q_{\max} = 41.15$ mg g⁻¹ means **1 gram of dry fungal biomass can sequester ~41 mg of Cd²⁺** — comparable to commercial ion-exchange resins, at a fraction of the cost.

---

## 3.3 Derivation: Monod-Limited Nutrient Removal in Algal PBR

**Problem:** In a *Spirulina* pond treating municipal wastewater, $K_s = 0.5$ mg L⁻¹ (for phosphate), $\mu_{\max} = 0.04$ h⁻¹, and residual phosphate $S = 0.2$ mg L⁻¹. Find μ and the % nutrient depletion.

**Step 1 — Apply Monod (Formula Sheet, Row 2):**

$$\mu = \mu_{\max} \cdot \dfrac{S}{K_{s} + S}$$

**Step 2 — Substitute:**

$$\mu = 0.04 \times \dfrac{0.2}{0.5 + 0.2} = 0.04 \times \dfrac{0.2}{0.7}$$

**Step 3 — Compute:**

$$\mu \approx 0.04 \times 0.2857 \approx 0.01143 \text{ h}^{-1}$$

**Step 4 — Removal efficiency** (assuming influent $S_0 = 5$ mg L⁻¹, $S = 0.2$ mg L⁻¹):

$$R\,\% = \dfrac{5 - 0.2}{5} \times 100 = 96\,\%$$

**Interpretation:** *Spirulina* is operating *below* $K_s$ ($S < K_s$), so growth is **phosphate-limited**. Effective for **tertiary wastewater polishing**.

```mermaid
    I --> I2[Biofertilizer]
    I --> I3[Animal Feed]
```

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    P[Pollutant: PAH / Dye / PCB] --> H[Fungal Hyphae Penetrate Soil Matrix]
    H --> E1[Lignin Peroxidase LiP]

    H --> E4[Cytochrome P450 Intracellular]

    P --> E2
```

# 5. KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

---

## PART A — Short Answer Questions (3 Marks Each)

### Q1. [KTU University Exam — May 2024]
**Differentiate between biosorption and bioaccumulation in algal bioremediation. Give one example for each.**

**Model Answer (3 marks):**

| Feature | Biosorption | Bioaccumulation |
|---|---|---|
| **Mechanism** | Passive binding of pollutants to the **algal cell wall** (functional groups: –COOH, –OH, –NH₂, –PO₄) | Active, **ATP-dependent** uptake of pollutants *into* the cytoplasm |
| **Metabolic state** | Independent of cell viability (works on **dead/live** biomass) | Requires **living, metabolically active** cells |
| **Speed** | **Fast** (minutes to hours) | **Slow** (hours to days) |
| **Reversibility** | **Reversible** (desorption possible) | Largely **irreversible** |
| **Example** | *Chlorella* dead biomass removing Cr(VI) via surface binding | *Spirulina* actively accumulating Cu²⁺ via Cu-ATPase transporters |

*(1 mark — one-line definition of each; 1 mark — mechanism/metabolism difference; 1 mark — example.)*

---

### Q2. [KTU University Exam — Dec 2023]
**What is the ligninolytic enzyme system? Name any two enzymes and their target pollutants.**

**Model Answer (3 marks):**
The **ligninolytic enzyme system** is a set of **extracellular, non-specific oxidative enzymes** secreted by white-rot fungi (e.g., *Phanerochaete chrysosporium*) to degrade **lignin** in wood. Due to the **structural similarity between lignin and many persistent organic pollutants (POPs)**, these enzymes can also co-oxidize a wide range of xenobiotics.

- **Lignin Peroxidase (LiP):** High redox potential (>1.4 V); degrades **PAHs** (e.g., benzo[a]pyrene), non-phenolic aromatics.
- **Laccase:** Cu-containing oxidase using O₂; decolorizes **azo dyes** and oxidizes **phenolic compounds** in textile wastewater.

*(1 mark — definition; 1 mark — any 2 enzymes; 1 mark — target pollutants.)*

---

## PART B — Long Answer Questions (14 Marks Each, Module Internal Choice)

### **Question A — 14 Marks** [KTU University Exam — May 2024]

**Phycoremediation is emerging as a sustainable alternative to conventional wastewater treatment. (a) Describe the various mechanisms by which algae remediate pollutants. (b) With a neat diagram, explain the working of an algal photobioreactor used for CO₂ sequestration. List its advantages over open raceway ponds.**

#### Part (a) — Mechanisms of Phycoremediation [7 marks]

**Model Answer:**

The five major mechanisms of algal bioremediation are:

1. **Biosorption [1.5 marks]:**
   - Passive, metabolism-independent binding of metal ions/dyes to the **negatively charged functional groups** of the algal cell wall (carboxyl, phosphate, sulfhydryl, hydroxyl).
   - Operates on **dead or dried biomass** — enables reuse and easy handling.
   - Mechanism involves **ion exchange, complexation, and electrostatic attraction**.

2. **Bioaccumulation [1.5 marks]:**
   - Active uptake of metals (Cd²⁺, Pb²⁺, Hg²⁺) **into the cytoplasm** via specific transporters (e.g., ZIP family, P-type ATPases).
   - **Metabolism- and energy-dependent** (requires ATP).
   - Risk: **Biomagnification** when contaminated biomass enters the food chain — must be safely disposed or used for non-food applications (e.g., biodiesel).

3. **Biotransformation / Biodegradation [1.5 marks]:**
   - Enzymatic conversion of organic pollutants (pesticides, dyes, phenols) into **less toxic metabolites**.
   - *Chlorella vulgaris* and *Scenedesmus* degrade **atrazine, malathion, and azo dyes** via cytochrome P450 and azoreductase enzymes.

4. **Biofixation [1.5 marks]:**
   - Conversion of inorganic pollutants (CO₂, NO₃⁻, NH₄⁺, PO₄³⁻) into **organic biomass** via photosynthesis and assimilation.
   - CO₂ → carbohydrates via **Calvin–Benson cycle**; N, P → proteins, nucleic acids, phospholipids.
   - **Dual benefit:** climate change mitigation + nutrient recovery.

5. **Rhizofiltration / Phytovolatilization [1 mark]:**
   - Algal mats/films filter contaminants from flowing water; some algae (e.g., *Chlorella*) can **methylate** toxic Se/As into volatile derivatives released to the atmosphere.

#### Part (b) — Photobioreactor (PBR) for CO₂ Sequestration [7 marks]

**Model Answer:**

**Definition [1 mark]:** A **Photobioreactor (PBR)** is a **closed, controlled cultivation vessel** designed for the photosynthetic growth of microalgae under optimized light, pH, temperature, and CO₂ conditions.

**Design / Diagram description [3 marks]:**

A **tubular PBR** consists of:
- An array of **transparent tubes** (glass/PLEXIGLAS), typically ≤ 0.1 m diameter (to maximize surface-area-to-volume ratio for light penetration).
- A **gas exchange / sparging column** at one end, where CO₂-enriched air (1–5% v/v) is bubbled.
- A **recirculation pump** to maintain turbulent flow (Reynolds number > 3000) preventing settling and biofouling.
- A **degasser** to remove O₂ (which inhibits photosynthesis above ~35 mg L⁻¹).
- **pH, temperature, and DO sensors** connected to a control unit.

**Working [2 marks]:**
1. CO₂-rich flue gas is sparged → dissolved as HCO₃⁻ → assimilated by algae via **Calvin cycle** → fixed as carbohydrates in biomass.
2. Sunlight (or LED panels) drives photophosphorylation → biomass growth.
3. Continuous circulation ensures uniform light exposure and gas exchange.
4. Harvested biomass is processed for biofuel, feed, or fertilizer.

**Advantages over Open Raceway Ponds [1 mark]:**
- Higher **biomass productivity** (up to 3–5 g L⁻¹ day⁻¹).
- **Lower contamination** risk (closed system).
- Better **CO₂ transfer efficiency** (>15% vs <5%).
- Reduced water evaporation and footprint.

---

### **Question B — 14 Marks** [KTU University Exam — Dec 2023]

**Mycoremediation is considered a powerful tool for degrading persistent organic pollutants. (a) Explain the ligninolytic enzyme system of white-rot fungi with suitable examples. (b) Describe the application of fungi in (i) dye decolorization and (ii) heavy metal biosorption.**

#### Part (a) — Ligninolytic Enzyme System [7 marks]

**Model Answer:**

**White-rot fungi** (e.g., *Phanerochaete chrysosporium, Trametes versicolor, Pleurotus ostreatus*) are the **only known organisms capable of mineralizing lignin completely** to CO₂ and H₂O. They secrete an **extracellular, non-specific, oxidative enzyme system** called the **ligninolytic enzyme system**.

**Why it works on pollutants:** Many POPs — **PAHs, PCBs, dioxins, chlorophenols, azo dyes, TNT, pesticides** — share **aromatic, ring-based, recalcitrant structures** resembling lignin. The ligninolytic enzymes **co-oxidize** these compounds with low substrate specificity.

**Key enzymes [5 marks]:**

1. **Lignin Peroxidase (LiP) [1.5 marks]:**
   - **Heme-containing glycoprotein**, requires H₂O₂.
   - Very high redox potential (>1.4 V); can oxidize **non-phenolic aromatic compounds**.
   - Degrades **benzo[a]pyrene, anthracene, pyrene** (PAHs).

2. **Manganese Peroxidase (MnP) [1.5 marks]:**
   - Heme peroxidase, oxidizes **Mn²⁺ → Mn³⁺**.
   - Mn³⁺ (chelated by organic acids like oxalate) diffuses into the lignified cell wall and attacks **phenolic substrates**.
   - Used for **chlorophenol and kraft lignin degradation**.

3. **Laccase (Lac) [1 mark]:**
   - **Multi-copper oxidase**; uses **molecular O₂** as the electron acceptor (no H₂O₂ needed).
   - Oxidizes **phenolic compounds and azo dyes** (textile effluent).
   - Industrial application: *Trametes versicolor* laccase decolorizes **Reactive Black 5** dye.

4. **Cytochrome P450 Monooxygenases [1 mark]:**
   - **Intracellular**; broad substrate range.
   - Hydroxylation of **PAHs, PCBs, alkanes**.

**Practical example [2 marks]:**
- *P. chrysosporium* immobilized on **polyurethane foam** in a CSTR has been shown to **degrade 80–95% of anthracene** (50 mg L⁻¹) within 7 days.
- *T. versicolor* laccase + mediator (HBT) system decolorizes >90% of **Indigo Carmine** in 2 hours.

#### Part (b) — Applications of Fungi [7 marks]

**(i) Dye Decolorization [3.5 marks]:**

- Textile industry releases **azo, anthraquinone, and triphenylmethane dyes** — many are **carcinogenic and recalcitrant**.
- **Mechanism:** Fungal laccases and peroxidases cleave the **chromophoric –N=N– (azo) bond**, breaking the dye into colourless aromatic amines.
- **Example:** *T. versicolor* decolorizes **Reactive Black 5, Congo Red, Methyl Orange** with >85% efficiency in 6–24 h.
- **Immobilization** on alginate beads or wood chips enables **reactor reuse for 10+ cycles**.

**(ii) Heavy Metal Biosorption [3.5 marks]:**

- Fungal cell wall components — **chitin, chitosan, glucans, melanins** — provide abundant **–OH, –NH₂, –COOH, –PO₄** groups.
- These bind heavy metals (Pb²⁺, Cd²⁺, Cr(VI), Hg²⁺, Ni²⁺) via **ion exchange, complexation, and precipitation**.
- **Industrial example:** *Aspergillus niger* biomass (a **waste product** from citric acid industry) — used as a **low-cost biosorbent** with q_max up to **40–60 mg g⁻¹** for Pb²⁺.
- **Process modes:** batch, packed-bed column, fluidized-bed reactor.
- **Advantages:** cheap, abundant, regenerable with dilute HNO₃ or EDTA.

> [!WARNING]
> **⚠ KTU Examiner's Valuation Pitfall — Read This Carefully!**
> - **Common Mistake 1:** Students write *"fungi absorb metals"* — wrong term. Use **biosorption** (abiotic/abiotic-like) vs **bioaccumulation** (active uptake). Fungal heavy metal removal is predominantly **biosorption**, not bioaccumulation.
> - **Common Mistake 2:** Confusing **ligninolytic** with **lignocellulosic** enzymes. Only the ligninolytic system (LiP, MnP, Lac) attacks pollutants. Cellulases, hemicellulases degrade **biomass**, not xenobiotics.
> - **Common Mistake 3:** Forgetting that **laccase uses O₂, while LiP/MnP require H₂O₂**. Examiners LOVE this distinction.
> - **Mark Loss Hot-Spot:** Skipping the **mediator role** in laccase (e.g., HBT, ABTS) — they expand the substrate range to non-phenolic compounds. Mentioning mediators = +1 mark guaranteed.

---

## 📌 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember (Rapid Revision Checklist)

- ✅ **Phycoremediation** = algae-based; **Mycoremediation** = fungi-based.
- ✅ Five algal mechanisms: **Biosorption, Bioaccumulation, Biotransformation, Biofixation, Rhizofiltration**.
- ✅ Fungal **ligninolytic enzymes**: **LiP, MnP, Laccase, P450**.
- ✅ **Laccase uses O₂**; **LiP and MnP use H₂O₂** — memorize this distinction.
- ✅ White-rot fungi are the **only** complete lignin mineralizers.
- ✅ Algae = **photoautotrophs** (need light + CO₂); Fungi = **heterotrophs** (need organic carbon).
- ✅ **q_max** is the key Langmuir parameter (mg of metal per g of biomass).
- ✅ Specific growth rate formula: $\mu = \dfrac{\ln X_2 - \ln X_1}{t_2 - t_1}$.
- ✅ **Biosorption** = passive, dead biomass, reversible, cell wall.
- ✅ **Bioaccumulation** = active, live biomass, cytoplasm, energy-dependent.
- ✅ Mycoremediation advantage: **extracellular enzymes attack large, insoluble POPs** bacteria cannot reach.
- ✅ Algal advantage: **dual benefit** — pollutant removal + CO₂ sequestration + biomass.
- ✅ Industrial fungal biosorbent: ***Aspergillus niger* waste biomass** from citric acid industry.
- ✅ *Chlorella* and *Spirulina* = most cited algal strains in KTU textbooks.
- ✅ *Phanerochaete chrysosporium* and *Trametes versicolor* = most cited fungal strains.
- ✅ Construction of $C_e/q_e$ vs $C_e$ plot → slope = $1/q_{\max}$ (Langmuir).
- ✅ **Biomagnification risk** is a key disadvantage of bioaccumulation.
- ✅ Mycoremediation coined/popularized by **Paul Stamets**.

# BIOMONITORING — Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

## 1.1 Formal Academic Definition (KTU 2024 Syllabus Standard)

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Biomonitoring** is the systematic, continuous observation and assessment of environmental quality and the presence, concentration, and biological effects of pollutants (xenobiotics, heavy metals, hydrocarbons, pesticides) using **living organisms — called bioindicators or sentinels — or their molecular/biochemical responses (biomarkers)** as natural measuring devices.

In the KTU 2024 Bioremediation framework (PEBBT754, Module 4), biomonitoring is positioned as the **feedback loop** that validates whether a bioremediation strategy has actually restored ecological health, beyond just reducing chemical concentrations. It connects **biological response data** (mortality, enzymatic induction, population shifts) with **environmental exposure data**.

### Sub-classifications of Biomonitoring

| Sub-type | Working Definition | KTU Scope |
|----------|-------------------|-----------|
| **Biomonitoring (senso stricto)** | Use of whole organisms (species, communities) | Module 4 — Core |
| **Biomarker assessment** | Use of biochemical / physiological / histological responses inside an organism | Module 4 — Core |
| **Bioaccumulation / Bioconcentration monitoring** | Measurement of pollutant uptake in tissues | Module 4 — Core |
| **Biosensing (biosensors)** | Device-integrated biological recognition element | Adjacent — Reference |

## 1.2 Conceptual Analogy — The "Canary in the Coal Mine"

Imagine you move into a new rented house. Instead of paying a laboratory to test every wall, pipe, and the air for toxins, you simply **bring in a sensitive houseplant**. If its leaves curl, yellow, or die within a few weeks, you infer the environment is toxic. If it thrives, the environment is safe.

The **canary in the coal mine** is the same logic at industrial scale — coal miners carried canaries into mines; if the canary died, it signalled lethal carbon monoxide long before the miners felt any effect.

In biomonitoring, the **canary = bioindicator organism** (lichens, daphnia, algae, fish, mussels). The plant's leaf-curl = the **biomarker** (e.g., acetylcholinesterase inhibition, metallothionein induction, DNA adducts).

> [!NOTE]
> **KTU High-Yield Mnemonic — "BRASS"**
> **B**ioindicator (organism-level)
> **R**esponse (behavioural / population)
> **A**ssay (biomarker)
> **S**entinel (transplanted test organism)
> **S**urvey (community-level ecological)

## 1.3 Why Biomonitoring is Non-Negotiable in Bioremediation

Chemical analysis alone tells you **"how much pollutant is left"** — but not **"is the ecosystem actually healed?"** A site may show **95% PAH degradation** on GC-MS while still being uninhabitable to native species due to residual toxicity. Biomonitoring closes this gap by measuring **ecological recovery in vivo**.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Syllabus Highlight (KTU 2024):** Biomonitoring is mandatory in the *post-bioremediation verification phase* for **PETL/CPCB guidelines** and is a recurring 14-mark question theme.
<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->
# SECTION 2 — Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

## 2.1 The Operational Logic of Biomonitoring — 6 Sequential Steps

Biomonitoring is not a single test — it is a **structured pipeline**. Each step has a specific KTU-examinable rationale.

### Step 1 — Hypothesis Formulation
**Why:** Define *what* you are monitoring (e.g., heavy-metal load in a river downstream of a paper mill) and *what biological endpoint* matters (mortality, reproduction, community diversity).
**How:** Compare baseline data from an **upstream control site** with the **impacted downstream site**.

### Step 2 — Selection of Bioindicator Species
**Why:** Not every organism is equally sensitive. The ideal bioindicator is:
- **Sensitive** to the target pollutant at sub-lethal concentrations.
- **Sessile or low-mobility** (so it reflects local conditions, not migration).
- **Abundant and easily identifiable**.
- **Well-known biology** (taxonomy, life-cycle, physiology).
- **Tolerant to handling** (for transplanted specimens).

**How — Canonical KTU Bioindicator Matrix:**

| Pollutant Class | Preferred Bioindicator | Tissue / Response |
|-----------------|----------------------|-------------------|
| Heavy metals (Cd, Pb, Hg) | *Daphnia magna*, *Lemna minor*, mosses | Whole body, fronds |
| PAHs / petroleum hydrocarbons | *Oncorhynchus mykiss* (rainbow trout), *Mytilus edulis* | Liver, gill |
| Pesticides (organophosphates) | Aquatic invertebrates, fish | AChE inhibition |
| Eutrophication / organic load | Diatoms, macroinvertebrates | Species diversity indices |
| Air quality (SO₂, NOₓ) | Lichens, *Tillandsia* (Spanish moss) | Chlorophyll degradation |
| Radiation | Pine trees, *Trichogramma* wasps | Mutation frequency |

### Step 3 — Active vs Passive Biomonitoring
This is the **most frequently asked conceptual distinction** in KTU exams.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Passive Biomonitoring** = observing the **naturally resident** organisms in situ. Measures *real, integrated* exposure over time but is limited to organisms actually present.
>
> **Active Biomonitoring (Transplant / Cage Studies)** = introducing **standardised, healthy test organisms** (often from a clean reference site) into the study area in cages or mesh bags. Enables **controlled, reproducible** comparison but introduces artefacts (caging stress, transport).

### Step 4 — Biomarker Selection
Biomarkers are classified by **biological organisation level**:

1. **Biochemical / Molecular biomarkers** — Enzyme induction (e.g., CYP4501A in fish exposed to PAHs), metallothionein (MT) for metals, acetylcholinesterase (AChE) inhibition for pesticides, DNA adducts.
2. **Physiological biomarkers** — Heart rate, respiration rate, scope-for-growth in mussels, photosynthesis rate in algae.
3. **Histological / Morphological biomarkers** — Gill lamellae erosion, liver vacuolation, micronuclei formation.
4. **Behavioural biomarkers** — Swimming speed, feeding rate, phototactic response, predator avoidance.
5. **Population / Community biomarkers** — Species richness, evenness, Index of Biotic Integrity (IBI).

### Step 5 — Sampling & Quantification
**How:** Standardised collection (e.g., Kick-net for macroinvertebrates, quadrat sampling for lichens), preservation (liquid nitrogen for enzymes), and analytical readout (spectrophotometry for AChE, AAS for metals in tissues, HPLC for PAH metabolites).

### Step 6 — Data Integration & Ecological Risk Assessment
**Why:** A biomarker signal must be translated into a **decision**: "Is the site safe?" or "Do we continue bioremediation?"
**How:** Combine chemical data, biomarker data, and community indices in a **Weight-of-Evidence (WoE)** approach — endorsed by **CPCB (India)** and **USEPA**.

## 2.2 KTU Formula Sheet / Cheat Sheet

> [!NOTE]
> **All formulas below are board-exam ready and frequently tested in numerical / 7-mark sub-parts.**

| # | Formula / Index | Expression | Application | Unit |
|---|-----------------|------------|-------------|------|
| 1 | **Bioconcentration Factor (BCF)** | $\text{BCF} = \dfrac{C_{\text{organism}}}{C_{\text{water}}}$ | Metal / PAH uptake | $\text{L}\cdot\text{kg}^{-1}$ |
| 2 | **Bioaccumulation Factor (BAF)** | $\text{BAF} = \dfrac{C_{\text{organism}}}{C_{\text{environment}}}$ | Field biomonitoring | dimensionless or $\text{L}\cdot\text{kg}^{-1}$ |
| 3 | **Biomagnification Factor (BMF)** | $\text{BMF} = \dfrac{C_{\text{predator}}}{C_{\text{prey}}}$ | Food-chain transfer | dimensionless |
| 4 | **Shannon Diversity Index ($H'$)** | $H' = -\sum_{i=1}^{S} p_i \, \ln p_i$ | Community monitoring | bits/individual |
| 5 | **Simpson's Index ($D$)** | $D = \sum_{i=1}^{S} p_i^{2}$ | Dominance | dimensionless |
| 6 | **Evenness ($J'$)** | $J' = \dfrac{H'}{\ln S}$ | Community structure | dimensionless |
| 7 | **Index of Biotic Integrity (IBI)** | IBI = $\sum$ of 12 metric scores | Stream health | 0 – 60 score |
| 8 | **% AChE Inhibition** | $\% \text{Inh} = \dfrac{A_{\text{control}} - A_{\text{sample}}}{A_{\text{control}}} \times 100$ | Pesticide biomarker | % |
| 9 | **HMPI (Heavy Metal Pollution Index)** | $\text{HMPI} = \dfrac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} M_{i} \, W_{i}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} W_{i}}$ | Multi-metal load | composite |
| 10 | **Biota-Sediment Accumulation Factor (BSAF)** | $\text{BSAF} = \dfrac{C_{\text{organism}}/f_{\text{lipid}}}{C_{\text{sediment}}/f_{\text{OC}}}$ | Sediment quality | dimensionless |

**Boundary conditions & KTU exam tips:**
- BCF $> 500$ $\text{L}\cdot\text{kg}^{-1}$ ⇒ substance is **bioaccumulative** (Stockholm Convention trigger).
- BCF $> 5000$ $\text{L}\cdot\text{kg}^{-1}$ ⇒ **very bioaccumulative (vB)**.
- AChE inhibition $>30\%$ ⇒ **significant neurotoxic impact**.
- Shannon $H' < 1.5$ ⇒ **highly degraded** community.
- $H' > 3.0$ ⇒ **healthy** community.
- IBI score: $\geq 48$ = good, $\leq 24$ = poor.

## 2.3 Real-World Engineering Utility

| Domain | Biomonitoring Use |
|--------|-------------------|
| **Municipal STP effluent validation** | *Daphnia* acute/chronic assays for CPCB consent |
| **Petroleum refinery bioremediation** | PAH biliary metabolites in fish; CYP4501A induction |
| **Mine-tailings reclamation** | Metallothionein levels in transplanted earthworms |
| **Pesticide manufacturing site** | AChE inhibition in resident fish |
| **Urban air-quality boards** | Lichen Diversity Value (LDV) mapping |
| **Wetland construction verification** | Macroinvertebrate IBI scoring |

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **KTU Examiner Pattern (2024):** Whenever a question asks "how will you *verify* a bioremediation outcome", the model answer should integrate **chemical + biomarker + community indices** — not just one of them.
<!-- SECTION_2_END -->

<!-- SECTION_3_START -->
# SECTION 3 — Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix

## 3.1 Derivation 1 — Bioconcentration Factor (BCF) from First Principles

**Problem Context (KTU Numerical Style):**
A freshwater mussel (*Lamellidens marginalis*) is exposed to cadmium in a polluted river. After 28 days of controlled exposure, the cadmium concentration in the mussel's soft tissue is measured as $8.4\,\text{mg}\cdot\text{kg}^{-1}$ wet weight. The dissolved Cd in water remains stable at $0.04\,\text{mg}\cdot\text{L}^{-1}$. Calculate the BCF and classify the bioaccumulation potential.

### Step-by-Step Logical Expansion

**Step 1 — Identify the steady-state assumption.**
Bioconcentration Factor assumes the organism has reached **equilibrium uptake**, meaning the influx of the pollutant equals the efflux (depuration + growth dilution).

**Step 2 — Write the governing partition relation.**
At equilibrium, the pollutant partitions between water and the organism's lipid/aqueous tissues with a constant ratio:

$$
C_{\text{organism}} \; \rightleftharpoons \; K_{\text{ow}} \cdot C_{\text{water}}
$$

This is the **1-octanol/water partition coefficient ($K_{\text{ow}}$)** analogue for biological tissue.

**Step 3 — Define BCF as the empirical equilibrium ratio.**

$$
\text{BCF} = \dfrac{C_{\text{organism,eq}}}{C_{\text{water,eq}}}
$$

**Step 4 — Unit-consistent substitution.**
Given: $C_{\text{organism}} = 8.4 \,\text{mg}\cdot\text{kg}^{-1}$, $C_{\text{water}} = 0.04 \,\text{mg}\cdot\text{L}^{-1}$.

$$
\text{BCF} = \dfrac{8.4 \,\text{mg}\cdot\text{kg}^{-1}}{0.04 \,\text{mg}\cdot\text{L}^{-1}}
$$

**Step 5 — Cancel mg and convert the denominator unit.**
Since $1 \,\text{kg}$ of water $\approx 1 \,\text{L}$, we keep the resulting unit as $\text{L}\cdot\text{kg}^{-1}$:

$$
\text{BCF} = 210 \,\text{L}\cdot\text{kg}^{-1}
$$

**Step 6 — Interpret against regulatory thresholds.**

| BCF Range $\left(\text{L}\cdot\text{kg}^{-1}\right)$ | Regulatory Class |
|---|---|
| $< 100$ | Not bioaccumulative |
| $100$ – $500$ | Borderline |
| $500$ – $5000$ | Bioaccumulative (**B**) |
| $> 5000$ | Very bioaccumulative (**vB**) |

**Step 7 — Conclude.**
BCF $= 210 \,\text{L}\cdot\text{kg}^{-1}$ ⇒ Cd in this mussel is **borderline bioaccumulative**. The mussel is a useful sentinel but not a strong accumulator.

---

## 3.2 Derivation 2 — Shannon Diversity Index from Probability Theory

**Problem Context (KTU Numerical Style):**
A post-bioremediation wetland is sampled for macroinvertebrates across 4 sampling stations. The species count data is:

| Species | Count ($n_i$) |
|---|---|
| Chironomus sp. | 38 |
| Tubifex sp. | 12 |
| Baetis sp. | 6 |
| Hydropsyche sp. | 4 |

Total individuals $N = 60$, total species $S = 4$.
Compute $H'$ and $J'$ and interpret.

### Step-by-Step Logical Expansion

**Step 1 — Compute the proportion $p_i$ for each species.**

$$
p_i = \dfrac{n_i}{N}
$$

$$
p_{\text{Chir}} = \dfrac{38}{60} = 0.6333
$$

$$
p_{\text{Tub}} = \dfrac{12}{60} = 0.2000
$$

$$
p_{\text{Bae}} = \dfrac{6}{60} = 0.1000
$$

$$
p_{\text{Hyd}} = \dfrac{4}{60} = 0.0667
$$

**Step 2 — Verify $\sum p_i = 1$.**

$$
0.6333 + 0.2000 + 0.1000 + 0.0667 = 1.0000 \;\checkmark
$$

**Step 3 — Apply the Shannon formula.**

$$
H' = -\sum_{i=1}^{S} p_i \cdot \ln p_i
$$

**Step 4 — Term-by-term expansion.**

$$
\begin{aligned}
H' &= - \bigl[\, 0.6333 \cdot \ln(0.6333) + 0.2000 \cdot \ln(0.2000) \\
   &\qquad + 0.1000 \cdot \ln(0.1000) + 0.0667 \cdot \ln(0.0667) \,\bigr]
\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 5 — Evaluate each natural log.**

$$
\ln(0.6333) = -0.4568
$$

$$
\ln(0.2000) = -1.6094
$$

$$
\ln(0.1000) = -2.3026
$$

$$
\ln(0.0667) = -2.7071
$$

**Step 6 — Multiply and sum.**

$$
\begin{aligned}
0.6333 \times (-0.4568) &= -0.2893 \\
0.2000 \times (-1.6094) &= -0.3219 \\
0.1000 \times (-2.3026) &= -0.2303 \\
0.0667 \times (-2.7071) &= -0.1806 \\
\text{Sum} &= -1.0221
\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 7 — Apply the negative sign.**

$$
H' = -(-1.0221) = 1.0221 \;\text{bits/individual}
$$

**Step 8 — Compute Evenness $J'$.**

$$
J' = \dfrac{H'}{\ln S} = \dfrac{1.0221}{\ln 4} = \dfrac{1.0221}{1.3863}
$$

$$
J' = 0.7373
$$

**Step 9 — Interpret.**
$H' = 1.022 < 1.5$ ⇒ **highly disturbed / polluted community** (per KTU thresholds).
$J' = 0.74$ ⇒ moderately even but skewed by Chironomus dominance (typical of organic-polluted, recovering sites).
**Conclusion:** Bioremediation has progressed chemically, but **ecological recovery is incomplete** — recommend extended biostimulation.

---

## 3.3 Analytical Matrix — Linking Pollutants to Biomarkers

| Pollutant Class | Exposure Route | Bioindicator | Biomarker | Diagnostic Threshold | KTU Cross-link |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **PAHs** | Gills, food | Fish (*Oncorhynchus*) | EROD / CYP4501A | $> 5\times$ induction | Module 2 |
| **Organophosphates** | Water, food | Fish, invertebrates | AChE inhibition | $> 30\%$ inhibition | Module 3 |
| **Heavy metals (Cd, Hg, Pb)** | Water, sediment | Mussels, earthworms | Metallothionein (MT) | $> 3\times$ basal MT | Module 2 |
| **PCBs / Dioxins** | Food chain | Birds (eggs), fish | Vitellogenin, EROD | Induction ratio $> 4$ | Module 3 |
| **Petroleum hydrocarbons** | Water column | *Daphnia*, algae | Feeding rate, photosynthesis | $> 25\%$ drop | Module 1 |
| **Nutrients (N, P)** | Runoff | Diatoms, macrophytes | Trophic Index (TI) | TI $> 3.5$ eutrophic | Module 4 |
| **Radiation** | Air, soil | Pine needles | Mutation frequency | Doubling vs control | Module 5 |

## 3.4 Worked Example — AChE Inhibition Calculation (Pesticide Biomarker)

**Problem:** Fish brain acetylcholinesterase (AChE) activity in control = $480\,\text{nmol}\cdot\text{min}^{-1}\cdot\text{mg}^{-1}$. Fish exposed to a malathion-impacted pond downstream of a bioremediation site show activity = $288\,\text{nmol}\cdot\text{min}^{-1}\cdot\text{mg}^{-1}$.

**Step 1 — Write the formula.**

$$
\% \text{ Inhibition} = \dfrac{A_{\text{control}} - A_{\text{sample}}}{A_{\text{control}}} \times 100
$$

**Step 2 — Substitute.**

$$
\% \text{ Inhibition} = \dfrac{480 - 288}{480} \times 100
$$

**Step 3 — Compute numerator.**

$$
480 - 288 = 192
$$

**Step 4 — Divide and convert.**

$$
\dfrac{192}{480} = 0.4000 \;\Rightarrow\; 0.4000 \times 100 = 40\%
$$

**Step 5 — Interpret.**
$40\%$ AChE inhibition falls in the **"severe effect"** category ($>30\%$).
**Conclusion:** Despite bioremediation activity, the site still poses neurotoxic risk; **continue phytoremediation polishing and additional carbon supplementation** for microbial degradation of malathion.

# SECTION 5 — KTU 2024 Scheme Examination Question Bank & Topic Recap

## 5.1 PART A — Short Answer Questions (3 Marks Each)

> **[KTU University Exam – Dec 2023, PEBBT754 Model Paper]**

### Question A1 (3 Marks)
**Differentiate between bioaccumulation and biomagnification. Give one example organism for each.**

**Model Answer:**
- **Bioaccumulation:** Net accumulation of a substance in an organism's body over time, from **all exposure routes** (water, food, sediment). Measured by the **Bioconcentration Factor (BCF)** or **Bioaccumulation Factor (BAF)**. Example: Mercury accumulation in tuna muscle.
- **Biomagnification:** Progressive **increase in concentration** of a substance **up the food chain**, from prey to predator. Measured by the **Biomagnification Factor (BMF)**. Example: DDT magnification in aquatic food web (water $\to$ zooplankton $\to$ fish $\to$ birds).

> [!WARNING]
> **Common 1-mark loss:** Students confuse BCF with BAF. **BCF = water only**; **BAF = all routes combined** (water + diet + sediment contact).

---

### Question A2 (3 Marks)
**What is the Index of Biotic Integrity (IBI) and why is it considered a holistic biomonitoring tool?**

**Model Answer:**
The **Index of Biotic Integrity (IBI)** is a **multi-metric scoring system** developed by Karr (1981) that evaluates **12 biological attributes** of a fish community — species richness, indicator species, trophic composition, individual health, etc. — assigning a score from **1 to 5** for each metric. Total IBI score ranges **0–60**.

It is considered holistic because it integrates **taxonomic, trophic, reproductive, and health dimensions** of an ecosystem into a single numerical index, allowing direct comparison across sites and time.

---

## 5.2 PART B — 14-Mark Questions (Module Internal Choice)

### ⭐ Question A (14 Marks) — Comprehensive Question
**[KTU University Exam – June 2024, PEBBT754]**

**A.** (a) Define biomonitoring and explain its role in the **post-bioremediation verification** of a petroleum-hydrocarbon contaminated site. Differentiate between **active and passive biomonitoring** with suitable examples. **(7 marks)**
**(b)** Describe in detail the **biochemical biomarkers** used in aquatic biomonitoring. With a neat sketch, explain the **acetylcholinesterase (AChE) inhibition pathway** in fish exposed to organophosphate pesticides. **(7 marks)**

#### Model Solution for A(a)

**Definition (1 mark):**
Biomonitoring is the use of biological organisms (bioindicators) and their molecular/cellular responses (biomarkers) to detect, quantify, and assess environmental pollutants and their biological effects.

**Role in post-bioremediation verification (3 marks):**
1. Confirms **ecological recovery**, not just chemical disappearance.
2. Validates compliance with **CPCB / USEPA** ecological standards.
3. Detects **residual toxicity** invisible to GC-MS (e.g., transformed intermediates).
4. Provides **public health assurance** (safe fish for consumption).
5. Generates **time-series recovery data** for adaptive management.

**Active vs Passive Biomonitoring (3 marks):**

| Feature | Passive Biomonitoring | Active Biomonitoring |
|---|---|---|
| Organism source | Naturally resident | Transplanted sentinel |
| Realism | High (integrated exposure) | Moderate (cage artefact) |
| Reproducibility | Low | High |
| Time frame | Long-term (decades) | Short-term (days–weeks) |
| Example | Lichen mapping around a refinery | *Mytilus* caged in cages at a refinery outfall |

#### Model Solution for A(b)

**Biochemical biomarkers list (3 marks):**
- **Cytochrome P4501A (CYP1A) / EROD** — PAH, dioxin, PCB exposure.
- **Metallothionein (MT)** — Cd, Hg, Zn, Cu exposure.
- **Acetylcholinesterase (AChE)** — Organophosphate & carbamate pesticide exposure.
- **Glutathione-S-transferase (GST)** — Phase-II detoxification.
- **DNA adducts / micronuclei** — Genotoxicity.
- **Vitellogenin** — Endocrine disruption.

**AChE inhibition pathway (4 marks):**
1. Organophosphate (OP) enters fish via gills / food.
2. OP binds **serine residue** in active site of **AChE enzyme**.
3. Enzyme becomes **phosphorylated** and cannot hydrolyse acetylcholine.
4. Acetylcholine accumulates at **neuromuscular junctions**.
5. Result: continuous nerve firing → **muscle fasciculation → paralysis → death**.
6. Measurement: Ellman spectrophotometric assay at **412 nm** using DTNB reagent.

> [!WARNING]
> **KTU Examiner Pitfall:** Students often write "AChE inhibits acetylcholine" — this is wrong. AChE **hydrolyses** acetylcholine; **inhibition of AChE** causes acetylcholine **accumulation**. State this clearly.

---

### ⭐ Question B (14 Marks) — Alternative Choice
**[KTU University Exam – Sample Paper, PEBBT754, KTU 2024 Scheme]**

**B.** (a) Define bioaccumulation factor (BAF). With a worked numerical example, compute the BAF of lead in *Pila globosa* (apple snail) and classify it. Comment on its use as a **biomonitoring tool**. **(7 marks)**
**(b)** Explain the **Shannon-Wiener diversity index** ($H'$) and its ecological interpretation. Compute $H'$ for a given dataset and comment on the **recovery status** of a bioremediated wetland. **(7 marks)**

#### Model Solution for B(a)

**Definition (2 marks):**
$$
\text{BAF} = \dfrac{C_{\text{organism}}}{C_{\text{environment}}}
$$
where $C_{\text{organism}}$ is the contaminant concentration in the organism ($\text{mg}\cdot\text{kg}^{-1}$) and $C_{\text{environment}}$ is the total concentration in the surrounding medium (water + sediment, expressed in compatible units).

**Numerical Problem (4 marks):**
Given:
- Pb in *Pila globosa* soft tissue, $C_{\text{org}} = 35\,\text{mg}\cdot\text{kg}^{-1}$
- Pb in surrounding pond water, $C_{\text{water}} = 0.10\,\text{mg}\cdot\text{L}^{-1}$

$$
\text{BAF} = \dfrac{35}{0.10} = 350\,\text{L}\cdot\text{kg}^{-1}
$$

**Classification:** BAF $= 350$ lies in the **borderline-to-bioaccumulative** range ($100$ – $500$).

**Use as biomonitoring tool (1 mark):**
*Pila globosa* is a sediment-dwelling, slow-moving gastropod with a wide Indo-Gangetic distribution — ideal as a **sentinel species** for freshwater heavy-metal biomonitoring, particularly in CPCB-monitored rivers of Kerala and Karnataka.

#### Model Solution for B(b)

**Definition (2 marks):**
$$
H' = -\sum_{i=1}^{S} p_i \ln p_i
$$
where $p_i$ is the proportion of individuals belonging to species $i$, and $S$ is the total species count.

**Ecological interpretation (2 marks):**
- $H' < 1.0$ ⇒ **severely polluted**
- $1.0 \le H' < 1.5$ ⇒ **highly degraded**
- $1.5 \le H' < 3.0$ ⇒ **moderate, recovering**
- $H' \ge 3.0$ ⇒ **healthy reference site**

**Worked example (3 marks):**
Given dataset:

| Species | Count |
|---|---|
| Species A | 25 |
| Species B | 15 |
| Species C | 5 |
| Species D | 3 |
| Species E | 2 |

$N = 50$, $S = 5$.

$$
p_A = 0.50, \quad p_B = 0.30, \quad p_C = 0.10, \quad p_D = 0.06, \quad p_E = 0.04
$$

$$
H' = -\bigl[0.50 \ln 0.50 + 0.30 \ln 0.30 + 0.10 \ln 0.10 + 0.06 \ln 0.06 + 0.04 \ln 0.04\bigr]
$$

$$
H' = -\bigl[-0.3466 - 0.3612 - 0.2303 - 0.1636 - 0.1288\bigr]
$$

$$
H' = 1.2305 \;\text{bits/individual}
$$

**Interpretation:** $H' = 1.23$ → falls in the **"highly degraded / early-recovery"** zone. The wetland shows **partial recovery** post-bioremediation; pollution-sensitive genera (Species D, E) are present but rare. **Recommendation:** Continue biostimulation + add riparian vegetation.

> [!WARNING]
> **KTU Examiner Pitfall (B(a)):** Students often write BAF = BCF. Remember: **BAF includes all routes** (water + food + sediment contact), while **BCF is water-only**. Numerical distinction is critical for full marks.

---

## 5.3 Topic Recap & Important Things to Remember

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **High-Density Revision Checklist — Biomonitoring (Module 4)**

- ✅ Biomonitoring = using **living organisms or biomarkers** to assess environmental quality.
- ✅ Two pillars: **Bioindicators (organism-level)** + **Biomarkers (molecular/cellular)**.
- ✅ Active biomonitoring = **transplanted sentinels**; Passive = **resident organisms**.
- ✅ Ideal bioindicator must be **sensitive, sessile, abundant, identifiable**.
- ✅ **Lichens** = air-quality sentinels; **Mussels** = aquatic sentinels; **Earthworms** = soil sentinels.
- ✅ **BCF** = water-only; **BAF** = all routes; **BMF** = predator/prey ratio.
- ✅ BCF $> 5000 \,\text{L}\cdot\text{kg}^{-1}$ ⇒ very bioaccumulative (regulatory trigger).
- ✅ **AChE inhibition** = biomarker for organophosphate/carbamate pesticides.
- ✅ **CYP4501A / EROD induction** = biomarker for PAHs, PCBs, dioxins.
- ✅ **Metallothionein (MT)** = biomarker for Cd, Hg, Zn, Cu.
- ✅ **Shannon $H' < 1.5$** = polluted; **$H' > 3.0$** = healthy.
- ✅ **IBI** integrates 12 fish-community metrics into a 0–60 score.
- ✅ Biomonitoring is the **WoE validation step** — never substitute it for chemical data, only integrate.
- ✅ In KTU answers, always combine **chemical + biomarker + community** evidence.
- ✅ Always mention **CPCB / USEPA** threshold for full marks in 14-mark questions.

---

### 🔖 Memory Anchor — Final 5-Word Summary
> **"Organism = Sensor; Biomarker = Response."**

> **APJ ABDUL KALAM TECHNOLOGICAL UNIVERSITY (KTU) | 2024 SCHEME**

> - **Module:** Module 4

<!-- SECTION_1_START -->
## 1. Core Technical Definition & Intuitive Overview

### 1.1 Formal Academic Definition

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Microbial enzymes in bioremediation** are biocatalysts (proteins or ribozymes) produced by bacteria, fungi, algae, or yeast that accelerate the breakdown, transformation, or detoxification of environmental pollutants including hydrocarbons, pesticides, dyes, plastics, heavy metals, and chlorinated compounds. These enzymes function under mild physiological conditions (ambient temperature, neutral pH, aqueous media) and replace conventional harsh physico-chemical treatment methods.

The **enzyme cocktail** secreted by microorganisms (intracellular, periplasmic, or extracellular) drives the catabolic pathways responsible for pollutant mineralization. The six major EC (Enzyme Commission) classes relevant to bioremediation are:

1. **EC 1 — Oxidoreductases**: Catalyze oxidation–reduction reactions.
2. **EC 2 — Transferases**: Transfer functional groups between molecules.
3. **EC 3 — Hydrolases**: Cleave bonds by addition of water.
4. **EC 4 — Lyases**: Cleave bonds by elimination (no water addition).
5. **EC 5 — Isomerases**: Catalyze geometric or structural rearrangements.
6. **EC 6 — Ligases**: Join two molecules via new covalent bonds (ATP-dependent).

> [!NOTE]
> **KTU 2024 Module 4 Highlight**: Special focus is laid on Oxidoreductases (laccases, peroxidases, mono/dioxygenases) and Hydrolases (lipases, proteases, cellulases) as these constitute the **"enzyme toolkit"** of bioremediation.

### 1.2 Conceptual Analogy / Intuition

Imagine a polluted river containing oil spills and plastic waste. The river is a "crime scene" of environmental contamination. Now, think of microbial enzymes as **molecular scissors and chemical blowtorches**:

- **Laccases / Peroxidases** act like **blowtorches** that oxidize stubborn aromatic rings in pesticides and dyes.
- **Hydrolases** act like **scissors** that snip the long chains of plastics, oils, and proteins into smaller, harmless pieces.
- **Monooxygenases** act like **targeted welders** that insert a single oxygen atom into hydrocarbons (e.g., converting toluene into benzyl alcohol).

Just as a locksmith uses specific tools to open specific locks, each enzyme has a specific substrate it acts upon. Microorganisms therefore deploy a *cocktail* of enzymes to tackle a *cocktail* of pollutants.

### 1.3 Key Standardized Metrics (Bold Highlights)

- **Enzyme Activity (U)**: 1 Unit = 1 μmol of substrate converted per minute.
- **Specific Activity**: Units per mg of protein (**U/mg**).
- **Turnover Number (k_cat)**: Molecules of substrate converted per enzyme molecule per second (**s⁻¹**).
- **KM (Michaelis Constant)**: Substrate concentration at half-maximal velocity (**mM** or **μM**).
- **Operational pH Range**: 4.0 – 9.0 (fungal enzymes often acidic; bacterial enzymes often neutral).
- **Operational Temperature**: 20 °C – 60 °C (mesophilic range).

<!-- SECTION_1_END -->

<!-- SECTION_2_START -->
## 2. Deep Theoretical Analysis & KTU High-Yield Formula Sheet

### 2.1 Classification of Pollutant-Degrading Microbial Enzymes

#### 2.1.1 Oxidoreductases (EC 1)

These are the **"workhorses"** of oxidative bioremediation, requiring cofactors such as NAD(P)H, FAD, or molecular oxygen.

| Enzyme | EC Subclass | Source Microorganisms | Target Pollutants |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Laccase** (benzenediol:oxygen oxidoreductase) | EC 1.10.3.2 | *Trametes versicolor*, *Pleurotus ostreatus*, *Bacillus subtilis* | PAHs, phenols, chlorophenols, synthetic dyes, lignin |
| **Manganese Peroxidase (MnP)** | EC 1.11.1.13 | *Phanerochaete chrysosporium* | Lignin, PAHs, chlorolignins |
| **Lignin Peroxidase (LiP)** | EC 1.11.1.14 | *Phanerochaete chrysosporium* | Non-phenolic aromatics, TNT, DDT |
| **Tyrosinase** | EC 1.14.18.1 | *Streptomyces*, *Agaricus bisporus* | Phenols, cresols, anilines |
| **Naphthalene Dioxygenase (NDO)** | EC 1.14.12.12 | *Pseudomonas putida* | PAHs (naphthalene → cis-1,2-dihydroxy-1,2-dihydronaphthalene) |
| **Monooxygenase (e.g., Cytochrome P450)** | EC 1.14.14.1 | *Pseudomonas*, *Rhodococcus* | Alkanes, toluene, chlorinated solvents |
| **Aryl-alcohol oxidase** | EC 1.1.3.7 | *Pleurotus eryngii* | Benzyl alcohols → aldehydes |

> [!NOTE]
> **Mechanism Highlight**: Laccase uses **4 Cu atoms** at its active site and reduces **O₂ → H₂O** while oxidizing the substrate. This makes it a "green" enzyme since the by-product is water, not hydrogen peroxide.

#### 2.1.2 Hydrolases (EC 3)

Catalyze bond cleavage by hydrolysis; do not require cofactors.

| Enzyme | EC Number | Target Substrate | Pollutant Application |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Lipase** | EC 3.1.1.3 | Ester bonds | Petroleum hydrocarbons, oil spills, biodiesel waste |
| **Protease** | EC 3.4.21.– | Peptide bonds | Protein-rich effluents (dairy, tannery, slaughterhouse) |
| **Phosphotriesterase (PTE)** | EC 3.1.8.1 | P–O bonds | Organophosphate pesticides (parathion, malathion) |
| **Cellulase** | EC 3.2.1.4 | β-1,4-glycosidic bonds | Agricultural lignocellulosic waste |
| **Esterase** | EC 3.1.1.1 | Carboxylic esters | Plasticizers (phthalates), xenobiotic esters |
| **Urease** | EC 3.5.1.5 | Urea | Heavy metal immobilization (ureolysis-driven CaCO₃ precipitation) |
| **Haloalkane Dehalogenase** | EC 3.8.1.5 | C–X bonds (X = Cl, Br, I) | Chlorinated solvents (1,2-dichloroethane) |

#### 2.1.3 Transferases, Lyases, and Isomerases

- **Glutathione S-transferase (GST)**: Conjugates glutathione to electrophilic xenobiotics (e.g., atrazine, chloroacetanilides) → water-soluble conjugates.
- **Ammonia Lyases**: e.g., aspartate ammonia lyase, histidine ammonia lyase — useful in amino-acid transformation of pollutant side-chains.
- **Cis-trans Isomerases**: Rearrangement of double bonds in unsaturated pollutants.

### 2.2 Applications — Pollutant-Specific Case Analysis

#### 2.2.1 Petroleum Hydrocarbon Degradation

- **Alkanes (C5–C40)**: Degraded by **alkane hydroxylases (AlkB)** and **cytochrome P450 monooxygenases**. Pathway: alkane → primary alcohol → aldehyde → fatty acid → β-oxidation → CO₂ + H₂O.
- **Aromatic Hydrocarbons (BTEX)**: Degraded by **toluene dioxygenase (TOD)** and **xylene monooxygenase (XMO)**.
- **PAHs (Polycyclic Aromatic Hydrocarbons)**: High-molecular-weight PAHs (4+ rings) are recalcitrant. **Lignin peroxidases** from white-rot fungi attack them by generating aryl cation radicals.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Industrial Application**: *Pseudomonas putida* GPo1 alk genes encode the **AlkBGT** enzyme system used commercially in oil-spill bioremediation kits.

#### 2.2.2 Pesticide Detoxification

- **Organophosphates** (parathion, malathion, chlorpyrifos): Cleaved by **organophosphohydrolase (OPH, EC 3.1.8.1)** and **phosphotriesterase** from *Pseudomonas diminuta*. Product: p-nitrophenol + dialkyl phosphate.
- **Organochlorines** (DDT, lindane, aldrin): Degraded by **dehalogenases** (EC 3.8.1.5) and **reductive dehalogenases** (anaerobic).
- **Carbamates** (carbaryl, carbofuran): Hydrolyzed by **carbamate hydrolase** (ICR, *Arthrobacter*).
- **Triazines** (atrazine): Dechlorinated and hydrolyzed by **atrazine chlorohydrolase (AtzA)** from *Pseudomonas sp. ADP*.

#### 2.2.3 Synthetic Dye Decolorization

Synthetic dyes (azo, anthraquinone, triphenylmethane) are major textile pollutants. Decolorization routes:

- **Azo dyes**: Cleavage of **–N=N–** bond by **azo reductase** (EC 1.7.1.6) using NADH as electron donor → aromatic amines.
- **Anthraquinone dyes**: Oxidized by **laccase** and **peroxidases**.
- **Phanerochaete chrysosporium** is a model white-rot fungus used for **80–95 % decolorization** of textile effluents.

#### 2.2.4 Plastic and Polymer Degradation

- **PET (Polyethylene Terephthalate)**: **PETase** (EC 3.1.1.101) from *Ideonella sakaiensis* hydrolyzes PET → MHET (mono-(2-hydroxyethyl) terephthalate) → MHETase → TPA + ethylene glycol.
- **Polyurethane (PU)**: **Urethanases / esterases** cleave carbamate and ester linkages.
- **Polyethylene**: Slow oxidative degradation by **laccases + mediators** (e.g., ABTS, HBT).

#### 2.2.5 Heavy Metal Transformation

Enzymes do not directly "destroy" metals (since metals are elements), but they **transform their redox state, solubility, and mobility**:

- **Mercury reductase (MerA)**: Hg²⁺ → Hg⁰ (volatile, removed by volatilization).
- **Arsenate reductase (ArsC)**: As⁵⁺ → As³⁺ (more mobile, then methylated by ArsM).
- **Chromate reductase (ChrR)**: Cr⁶⁺ → Cr³⁺ (less toxic, precipitates at neutral pH).
- **Urease-driven bioprecipitation**: Urea → NH₃ + CO₂ → CO₃²⁻ → precipitates Cd²⁺, Pb²⁺, Sr²⁺ as carbonates.

#### 2.2.6 Chlorinated Compound Dechlorination

- **LinA** (γ-hexachlorocyclohexane dehydrochlorinase) from *Sphingomonas paucimobilis* degrades **lindane (HCH)**.
- **Dehalococcoides spp.** use **reductive dehalogenases** to dechlorinate PCE → TCE → DCE → vinyl chloride → ethene.

## 3. Step-by-Step Derivations & Analytical Matrix

### 3.1 Derivation: Michaelis–Menten Equation (1913)

**Starting Model** (Briggs–Haldane steady-state assumption):

$$E + S \underset{k_{-1}}{\overset{k_1}{\rightleftharpoons}} ES \underset{k_{-2}}{\overset{k_{cat}}{\rightleftharpoons}} E + P$$

**Step 1 — Rate of product formation**:

$$v = \dfrac{d[P]}{dt} = k_{cat} \cdot [ES]$$

**Step 2 — Steady-state assumption for ES**:

$$\dfrac{d[ES]}{dt} = 0 = k_1 \cdot [E][S] - (k_{-1} + k_{cat}) \cdot [ES]$$

**Step 3 — Solve for [ES]**:

$$
[ES] = \dfrac{k_1 \cdot [E][S]}{k_{-1} + k_{cat}}
$$

**Step 4 — Define Michaelis constant**:

$$
K_M = \dfrac{k_{-1} + k_{cat}}{k_1}
$$

Substituting:

$$
[ES] = \dfrac{[E][S]}{K_M}
$$

**Step 5 — Total enzyme conservation**:

$$
[E]_T = [E] + [ES] \quad \Longrightarrow \quad [E] = [E]_T - [ES]
$$

**Step 6 — Substitute into [ES] equation**:

$$
[ES] = \dfrac{([E]_T - [ES])[S]}{K_M}
$$

Multiplying both sides by $K_M$:

$$
K_M \cdot [ES] = [E]_T \cdot [S] - [ES] \cdot [S]
$$

Rearranging to isolate [ES]:

$$
[ES] (K_M + [S]) = [E]_T \cdot [S]
$$

Therefore:

$$
[ES] = \dfrac{[E]_T \cdot [S]}{K_M + [S]}
$$

**Step 7 — Substitute back into v = k_cat · [ES]**:

$$
v = \dfrac{k_{cat} \cdot [E]_T \cdot [S]}{K_M + [S]}
$$

**Step 8 — Define V_max**:

$$
V_{max} = k_{cat} \cdot [E]_T
$$

**Final Michaelis–Menten Equation**:

$$
\boxed{v = \dfrac{V_{max} \cdot [S]}{K_M + [S]}}
$$

**Engineering Interpretation**: At low $[S] \ll K_M$, the rate is first-order in substrate: $v \approx (V_{max}/K_M)[S]$. At high $[S] \gg K_M$, the rate saturates to $V_{max}$, meaning the enzyme is the **rate-limiting** factor.

---

### 3.2 Derivation: Lineweaver–Burk Linearization

**Start** with the Michaelis–Menten equation:

$$
v = \dfrac{V_{max} [S]}{K_M + [S]}
$$

**Step 1 — Take reciprocal of both sides**:

$$
\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{K_M + [S]}{V_{max} [S]}
$$

**Step 2 — Split the fraction**:

$$
\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{K_M}{V_{max} [S]} + \dfrac{[S]}{V_{max} [S]}
$$

**Step 3 — Simplify the second term**:

$$
\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{K_M}{V_{max}} \cdot \dfrac{1}{[S]} + \dfrac{1}{V_{max}}
$$

**Final Lineweaver–Burk Equation**:

$$
\boxed{\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{K_M}{V_{max}} \cdot \dfrac{1}{[S]} + \dfrac{1}{V_{max}}}
$$

**Engineering Utility**: A plot of $1/v$ vs $1/[S]$ gives:
- y-intercept $= 1/V_{max}$
- x-intercept $= -1/K_M$
- slope $= K_M/V_{max}$

Inhibitor analysis:
- **Competitive inhibition**: Lines intersect on the y-axis ($V_{max}$ unchanged, $K_M$ increases).
- **Non-competitive inhibition**: Lines intersect on the x-axis ($K_M$ unchanged, $V_{max}$ decreases).
- **Uncompetitive inhibition**: Parallel lines (both $V_{max}$ and $K_M$ decrease).

---

### 3.3 Derivation: Immobilization Efficiency

**Step 1 — Define initial protein content in free enzyme**:

$$
P_{\text{free}} = \text{protein (mg) in enzyme solution before immobilization}
$$

**Step 2 — Define protein in supernatant (unbound enzyme)**:

$$
P_{\text{sup}} = \text{protein (mg) measured in wash + supernatant}
$$

**Step 3 — Protein bound to carrier**:

$$
P_{\text{imm}} = P_{\text{free}} - P_{\text{sup}}
$$

**Step 4 — Immobilization yield**:

$$
\text{Yield (\%)} = \dfrac{P_{\text{free}} - P_{\text{sup}}}{P_{\text{free}}} \times 100
$$

**Step 5 — Activity recovery**:

$$
\text{Activity Recovery (\%)} = \dfrac{\text{Activity of immobilized enzyme}}{\text{Activity of free enzyme loaded}} \times 100
$$

---

### 3.5 Numerical Worked Example (KTU-Style)

**Problem**: A laccase solution has $V_{max} = 200 \, \mu\text{mol·L}^{-1}\text{·min}^{-1}$ and $K_M = 0.5 \, \text{mM}$ for the dye Remazol Brilliant Blue R. Calculate the initial reaction velocity at $[S] = 2 \, \text{mM}$ and at $[S] = 0.1 \, \text{mM}$. What is the percentage saturation at each concentration?

**Solution**:

At $[S] = 2$ mM:

$$
v = \dfrac{200 \times 2}{0.5 + 2} = \dfrac{400}{2.5} = 160 \, \mu\text{mol·L}^{-1}\text{·min}^{-1}
$$

$$
\text{Saturation} = \dfrac{160}{200} \times 100 = 80\%
$$

At $[S] = 0.1$ mM:

$$
v = \dfrac{200 \times 0.1}{0.5 + 0.1} = \dfrac{20}{0.6} = 33.33 \, \mu\text{mol·L}^{-1}\text{·min}^{-1}
$$

$$
\text{Saturation} = \dfrac{33.33}{200} \times 100 = 16.67\%
$$

**Engineering Insight**: At $[S] \ll K_M$, doubling the substrate doubles the rate. At $[S] \gg K_M$, the rate is independent of substrate concentration, indicating enzyme saturation.

### 5.1 PART A — Short Answer Questions (3 Marks Each)

**Q1. [KTU University Exam – Model Question, 2024 Scheme]**
Define microbial enzymes and list the six major EC classes of enzymes with one bioremediation-relevant example of each.

**Model Answer**:
Microbial enzymes are protein catalysts produced by microorganisms that accelerate the breakdown of environmental pollutants. The six EC classes are:
- **EC 1 Oxidoreductases** — Laccase, peroxidase (degrades phenols, dyes, PAHs).
- **EC 2 Transferases** — Glutathione S-transferase (conjugates atrazine).
- **EC 3 Hydrolases** — Lipase, PETase, organophosphohydrolase.
- **EC 4 Lyases** — Aspartate ammonia lyase.
- **EC 5 Isomerases** — Cis-trans isomerases.
- **EC 6 Ligases** — Ubiquitin ligases (less common in bioremediation).

Explain the role of laccase in bioremediation. Mention its cofactor, active site, and one industrial application.

**Model Answer**:
Laccase (EC 1.10.3.2) is a multi-copper oxidase that catalyzes the one-electron oxidation of phenolic substrates, reducing molecular oxygen to water. Its active site contains **4 Cu atoms (T1, T2, T3)**. Industrial application: **decolorization of textile dyes** (azo, anthraquinone) and **biobleaching of paper pulp**.
